quiz.p: Divya, a girl in Class 3, floats a leaf in the middle of a bucket and taps the water at one side. What does the leaf do?
opts: It sails to the far side
It bobs up and down and stays near the middle
quiz.why: The ripples pass under the leaf, so the leaf bobs up and down. The ripples carry energy, not water, so the leaf stays near the middle. 'Sails to the far side' is what happens when you blow on the water, which pushes the water itself.

opts: Water moving from one place to another
Energy travelling through a material while the material stays in place
Anything that goes up and down
quiz.why: A wave is travelling energy. The material, such as water or a rope, moves a little and stays where it is. A swing goes up and down too, but nothing travels from it, so going up and down is not enough to make a wave.

quiz.p: Kavya, a girl in Class 3, sends the same wave across a tray. First the water is 1 cm deep, then 4 cm deep. When is the wave faster?
quiz.why: Deeper water carries this kind of wave faster. In 4 cm of water it goes about twice as fast as in 1 cm. If you picked 'the same', you may be thinking the push sets the speed. The push was the same both times, but the water was not.

quiz.p: In the Tray Test, why must you push the water the same way every time?
opts: So that only the depth changes, and we know the depth made the difference
So the water does not spill
quiz.why: In a fair test only one thing changes. If the push changed too, we could not tell whether the depth or the push made the wave faster.

quiz.p: Which of these is NOT a wave?
opts: A Mexican wave at a cricket match
Water flowing out of a tap
quiz.why: Water from a tap travels, so it is a flow, not a wave. In a Mexican wave and in ripples, the energy travels while the people or the water stay in place.

quiz.p: A Mexican wave runs round a stadium. What do the people do?
opts: Each person stands up and sits down in their seat
quiz.why: Each person stays in their seat. The standing up is passed from one person to the next, and that is what travels round.

quiz.p: What is the crest of a wave?
quiz.why: The crest is the top of a wave. The lowest point is the trough. The distance from one crest to the next is the wavelength.

quiz.p: Ripples on a bucket have a crest every 2 cm. What is their wavelength?
quiz.why: The wavelength is the distance from one crest to the next, so it is 2 cm. If you picked 1 cm, you measured from a crest to a trough, which is only half a wavelength.

quiz.p: A tsunami comes into shallow water near a beach. What happens to it?
opts: It slows down and grows taller
It speeds up and gets lower
quiz.why: In shallow water the wave slows down, just as in the Tray Test. The water behind is still in deeper water and moving faster, so it catches up and the wave piles up taller.

quiz.p: Fishermen far out at sea, in deep water, sometimes did not notice the 2004 tsunami passing under their boats. Why?
opts: In deep water the tsunami was low and very long
Boats cannot float on a tsunami
quiz.why: In deep water a tsunami is less than a metre high and more than 100 kilometres long, so a boat only rises and falls very gently. It grows tall only near the shore.

quiz.p: Inge Lehmann found a solid ball at the centre of the Earth. How?
opts: She studied the times when earthquake waves arrived at machines around the world
quiz.why: Nobody can dig that deep. Lehmann studied when earthquake waves arrived at seismographs far away. Faint waves arrived where a fully liquid core would leave none, so she worked out that the core has a solid ball inside.

quiz.p: Before 1936, what did many scientists think about the Earth's core?
opts: It was liquid all the way through
quiz.why: Many scientists thought the whole core was liquid metal. Inge Lehmann showed that a solid inner core explained the faint waves better. Later measurements in 1970 confirmed it.

items.p: Nila, a girl in Class 3, flicks one end of a dupatta tied to a door handle. A clothes peg is clipped in the middle. What does the peg do as the bump passes?
items.why: The bump passes through the cloth, and the peg jumps up and falls back where it was. Only the energy travels to the door.
opts: It slides along to the door
It jumps up and falls back in the same place

items.p: Energy travelling through a material, while the material stays in place, is called a ____.
items.why: A wave carries energy. The water, rope or air it travels through stays where it is.

items.p: The material a wave travels through, such as water or air, is called the ____.
items.why: The medium can be water, a rope, the air, rock or even a crowd of people.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
items.why: These words come up all through the unit.
pairs: the highest point of a wave
the lowest point of a wave
the distance from one crest to the next
the material a wave travels through
a long, fast sea wave started by an earthquake

items.p: Sort these. Is each one a wave, or is the stuff itself moving?
items.why: In a wave, the energy travels and the material stays. In the others, the thing itself moves from place to place.

items.p: When you blow across a bucket through a straw, the floating puffed rice sails away. This shows that waves carry water.
items.why: False. Blowing pushes the top of the water itself, like wind making a current. When you only tapped, the ripples crossed but the puffed rice stayed near the middle.

items.p: In a Mexican wave, every person stays in their own seat.
items.why: True. Each person only stands up and sits down. The standing up travels round the stadium.

items.p: In the Tray Test, the wave took 5 seconds at 1 cm and 3 seconds at 4 cm, with the same push. What does this show?
items.why: A shorter time means a faster wave. The wave was faster in 4 cm of water, and the push did not change, so the depth made the difference.
opts: Deeper water carries the wave faster
Shallow water carries the wave faster

items.p: Which of these could you use as a medium for a wave at home?
items.why: A wave can travel through cloth, water, a spring and many other materials.

items.p: Farhan, a boy in Class 3, taps the side of a bowl of water and a bowl of set curd. Where do the waves last longer?
items.why: In water, ripples run across and bounce for a few seconds. Thick curd soaks up the energy, so its wobble stops almost at once. Different materials carry waves differently.

items.p: Why did you shine a torch at a slant across the tray?
items.why: Light bends as it passes through the bump of the wave, making a bright line on the tray's bottom. That line is much easier to follow than the clear water.
opts: So the wave makes a bright line on the bottom that is easy to see

items.p: Label the drawing of a wave: crest, trough, wavelength, height.
items.why: The crest is the top, the trough is the bottom, the wavelength goes from one crest to the next, and the height goes from the flat line up to the crest.
items.art: A wavy line with a dotted flat line through its middle and four blank label lines pointing to a top, a bottom, a crest-to-crest gap and a flat-line-to-crest gap.

items.p: Tell how you would show a friend that ripples do not carry the water with them. What would you use, and what would they see?
items.a: Float puffed rice or paper in the middle of a bucket. Tap the water at one side. The ripples cross the bucket, but the puffed rice only bobs up and down and stays near the middle.
items.why: A strong answer names a floating thing, says how to make the waves without pushing the water, and says what the floating thing does.

items.p: Meenakshi saw a Mexican wave at Chepauk stadium. She said, 'The wave travelled, but nobody went anywhere.' How can both be true?
items.a: Each person only stood up and sat down in their own seat. The standing up was passed from person to person, so the wave travelled round while the people stayed.
items.why: A strong answer says what each person did and what travelled.

items.p: Draw a dupatta with a bump on it. Draw one arrow to show which way the bump travels, and another to show which way a clothes peg on it moves.
items.a: The bump arrow points along the dupatta towards the door. The peg arrow points up and down.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that the bump and the peg move in different directions: the bump along, the peg up and down.
items.art: A blank box with a door handle drawn on the right side.

items.p: Arjun, a boy in Class 3, says, 'If I push harder in the Tray Test, the wave will cross faster.' What would test his idea fairly?
items.why: To test the push, only the push may change. If the depth changed too, you could not tell which one made the difference.
opts: Push harder and make the water deeper at the same time
Keep the depth the same, and try a small push and a big push

items.p: A wave in the tray takes 3 seconds to go there and back once. How long would three trips there and back take?
items.why: Each trip takes 3 seconds. Three trips take 3 + 3 + 3 = 9 seconds, or 3 times 3.

items.p: When you make a shake wave on a spring toy, how does a paper tag on one coil move?
items.why: In a shake wave the coils move sideways and back while the bump travels along. The tag moves with its coil, then comes back.
opts: Sideways and back, across the spring
Along the spring to the far end
It does not move at all

items.p: In the straw wave machine, why did the wave slow down when it reached the straws with dough on their ends?
items.why: Heavy-ended straws are slower to start turning, so they pass the twist on more slowly. The material sets the speed, as the depth did in the tray.
opts: The heavy straws pass the twist on more slowly

items.p: A garden spider sits in the middle of her web. How does she know where an insect has landed?
items.why: Many web-building spiders see poorly. The spider rests her legs on the threads, and the waves from a struggling insect tell her which way to run.
opts: She sees it with her sharp eyes
She feels the waves of shaking along the threads with her legs

items.p: Put these in order, from where a wave would travel slowest to fastest.
items.why: Deeper water carries a long water wave faster.

items.p: A tsunami is tallest far out in the deep ocean.
items.why: False. In the deep ocean a tsunami is fast but less than a metre high. It slows down and grows tall only as the sea gets shallow near the shore.

items.p: Two sets of ripples can cross each other and both carry on.
items.why: True. Where they meet they add up for a moment, then each carries on as before. Two balls would bump, but two waves pass through each other.

items.p: When a wave hits a wall and bounces back, we say it ____.
items.why: A wave reflects from a wall. That is why the tray wave came back to you, and why you hear an echo.

items.p: Three of these are waves. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: The paper boat is carried by water that is itself flowing. In the other three, energy travels while the material stays.
opts: A squeeze running along a spring toy
Sound from a pressure cooker whistle
A paper boat carried down a gutter by rainwater
Shaking that travels through the ground in an earthquake

items.p: Lakshmi and her grandmother are at Marina Beach in Chennai, watching the waves come in.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side, uses evidence from the bucket or tray, and fairly says what the other person has right.
items.why: Both have part of the truth. Far out, the water mostly goes round in small circles. Where waves break near the beach, water really does rush up the sand.

views.says: The waves are bringing water from far out at sea to the beach.
The water stays out there. Only the waves come in. Look at that fishing boat, just bobbing.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Give a reason from your bucket experiment. Then say one thing the other person has right.

items.p: Kavya's Tray Test: 1 cm took 6 seconds, 2 cm took 4 seconds, 4 cm took 3 seconds. Write what pattern you see, and predict what happens at 6 cm.
items.a: The deeper the water, the shorter the time, so the faster the wave. At 6 cm, the time would be a little shorter than 3 seconds.
items.why: A strong answer states the pattern in words and makes a prediction that follows it, without guessing a time below zero or a big jump.

items.p: In the family stadium wave, the wave was slower when everyone counted 'one, two' before standing. The first person started it the same way both times. What does this tell you about what sets a wave's speed?
items.a: The speed was set by how quickly each person passed it on, not by the person who started it. So the medium, here the people, sets the speed of a wave.
items.why: A strong answer connects the speed to the people in the line and not to the start.

items.p: A crow sits on a pond as ripples pass. Say what the crow will do, and why.
items.a: The crow will bob up and down as each ripple passes, but stay in about the same place, because ripples carry energy, not water.
items.why: A strong answer uses the idea that the water stays in place.

items.p: Draw a tray seen from the side, with water in it. Draw a wave travelling across it, and label the crest and the trough.
items.a: A side view of a tray with a wavy water surface, the top labelled crest and the bottom labelled trough.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the water level, the wave shape, and both labels in the right places.
items.art: A blank box with the outline of an empty tray drawn from the side.

items.p: Two trays have water 4 cm deep. Tray A is 30 cm long and tray B is 60 cm long. The same wave goes there and back once in each. Which takes longer?
items.why: The depth is the same, so the wave goes at the same speed. Tray B is twice as long, so the trip takes about twice as long.
opts: Tray B, about twice as long

items.p: A tsunami travels about 800 km in an hour over the deep ocean. Near the shore it slows to about 40 km in an hour. Why does it slow down?
items.why: Like the wave in your tray, a tsunami slows down in shallow water. It still carries most of its energy, which is why it grows tall and dangerous.
opts: The water near the shore is shallow
The wave runs out of energy

items.p: Sound goes faster through steel than through air. What does this tell you?
items.why: Sound waves, like water waves, travel at a speed set by the material they pass through.
opts: The material sets the speed of a wave

items.p: In 1929, a big earthquake shook New Zealand. Machines on the far side of the world recorded faint waves where a fully liquid core would leave none. What did Inge Lehmann conclude?
items.why: Lehmann showed that a solid inner core would bend the waves so that some reach those places. More sensitive machines confirmed this in 1970.
opts: The core has a solid ball inside it

items.p: Divya pushes the water in a tray once. The wave fades after one trip. What would help her see it for longer?
items.why: In very shallow water, rubbing against the bottom takes the wave's energy quickly. In deeper water the wave lasts longer. A torch at a slant also helps.
opts: Use deeper water, so the bottom slows the wave less

items.p: Sort these waves by what they travel through.
items.why: A medium can be a liquid, a solid or a gas like air. Light is special: it can cross empty space.
items: a spider feeling her web shake

items.p: Put these in the order they happened.
a: A big earthquake shakes New Zealand
Inge Lehmann publishes her paper on the inner core
More sensitive machines pick up waves bouncing off the inner core
items.why: The earthquake was in 1929, Lehmann's paper in 1936, and the confirmation in 1970.
items: Inge Lehmann publishes her paper on the inner core
More sensitive machines pick up waves bouncing off the inner core
A big earthquake shakes New Zealand

items.p: In a wave, the push that starts it sets its speed, and the material only carries it.
items.why: False. In the Tray Test the same push went at different speeds in different depths. The material sets the speed. The push mostly sets how tall the wave is.

items.p: Machines that record earthquake waves are called ____.
items.why: Seismographs in many countries record when earthquake waves arrive. Scientists use the times to see inside the Earth.

items.p: After the 2004 tsunami, a village in Tamil Nadu is deciding how to protect its coast.
items.a: A strong answer picks a plan, gives a reason from the unit or the Save the Clay Village challenge, and fairly states one strength of another plan.
items.why: There is no single right answer. Walls block waves but cost a lot and can fail. Mangroves calm everyday waves and give fish a home, but scientists argue about how much they help in a big tsunami. Warnings save lives whatever the coast looks like.

views.says: Build a strong sea wall. It blocks the waves before they reach the houses.
Plant mangrove forests along the shore. They calm the waves and the fish breed among their roots.
Teach everyone the warning signs, like the sea pulling back, and build a path to high ground.

items.ask: Which plan would you choose first? Give a reason. Then say what is good about one of the other plans.

items.p: Look at the habit: 'Whoever starts something decides how fast it goes.' Use the Tray Test or the stadium wave to explain why this is not true for a wave.
items.a: In the Tray Test, the push was the same every time, but the wave went at different speeds in different depths. So after the start, the water decides the speed. In the stadium wave, the start was the same, but a slow crowd made a slow wave.
items.why: A strong answer uses real evidence from the child's own test and says clearly what sets the speed.

items.p: Your voice reaches a friend across a room as a wave in the air. Has any of the air from your mouth reached them? Explain using what you saw with the puffed rice.
items.a: Almost none. The air near your mouth only moves back and forth a tiny bit and passes the energy on, like the water passing ripples under the puffed rice. What reaches your friend is the energy of the wave.
items.why: A strong answer links sound to the puffed rice result and says what travels and what stays.

items.p: Why do you think a tsunami warning centre needs to know how deep the sea is?
items.a: Because the speed of the tsunami depends on the depth of the sea. Knowing the depth, they can work out when the wave will reach each part of the coast and warn people in time.
items.why: A strong answer connects depth to speed and speed to arrival time.

items.p: In the bucket, the puffed rice crept forward about 1 cm. Kavya says, 'So waves do carry water after all.' What would you say to her?
items.a: The puffed rice moved only a centimetre while the ripples crossed the whole bucket. The water mostly goes round in small circles, and each circle ends slightly forward, so floating things creep a little. But the wave's energy went much further than the water did.
items.why: A strong answer takes Kavya's evidence seriously, compares the distances, and explains the small creep.

items.p: Draw the Earth cut in half. Show the crust, the mantle, the liquid outer core and the solid inner core. Draw one earthquake wave bending as it goes through.
items.a: A circle with layers from outside to inside: crust, mantle, liquid outer core, solid inner core, and a curved line through them.
items.why: A strong drawing has the four layers in the right order and a wave path that bends where layers meet.
items.art: A blank circle with a small star on its edge to mark an earthquake.

applications: Tsunami warning centres, like the one in Hyderabad, use the depth of the sea to work out when a wave will reach each part of the coast.
Seismologists use earthquake waves to map the inside of the Earth and to find oil and water underground.
Doctors use sound waves in an ultrasound scan to see a baby inside the mother, or to look at a heart.
Breakwaters at harbours such as Chennai and Visakhapatnam calm the waves so ships can load safely.
Engineers design buildings in earthquake zones so that earthquake waves shake them without breaking them.
Phones, radios and television use waves to carry messages without any wire.
Some places are testing machines that turn the energy of sea waves into electricity.

open_questions.q: What exactly is at the very centre of the Earth?
open_questions.why_open: Some scientists think the solid inner core has a different innermost part at its centre, found from earthquake waves. Others are not sure yet, because few waves pass right through the middle.

open_questions.q: Why do giant 'rogue waves' suddenly appear at sea?
open_questions.why_open: Sailors have long told of single waves much taller than the rest. Scientists have measured them, and have several ideas about how they form, but cannot yet say exactly when one will appear.

open_questions.q: Can we know a tsunami is coming before the earthquake starts it?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can warn after an earthquake, but nobody can yet predict when an earthquake will happen.

open_questions.q: Do some animals really sense earthquakes and tsunamis before people do?
open_questions.why_open: There are many stories, including after 2004, but they are hard to test, and scientists still disagree about what the animals were sensing.

If you could not dig into the ground, how could you find out what is under your building?
Where have you seen waves today?

Why did the ripple never get lost?
jokes.a: Because it always came back from the wall.

jokes.j: Why was the Mexican wave so tired?
jokes.a: Everyone kept passing it on to someone else.

jokes.j: What do you call a wave that won't go anywhere?

jokes.a: It only liked to bob along with friends.

jokes.j: What did one wave say to the other wave?

maths.problem: In the Tray Test, Meenakshi timed the wave at 1 cm three times: 5.4 seconds, 5.1 seconds and 5.6 seconds. What is the middle time?
maths.explain: Put the times in order: 5.1, 5.4, 5.6. The one in the middle is 5.4 seconds. The middle time stops one late press of the stopwatch from changing the answer too much.
maths.why_maths: Three tries give three slightly different numbers. The middle one is a fair single answer.
maths.context: This is about the Tray Test, where you time a wave across a tray and back.

maths.problem: A Mexican wave travels about 20 seats each second. One stand has 100 seats in a row. About how long does the wave take to cross the stand?
maths.explain: 20 seats in 1 second. 40 seats in 2 seconds. 60 in 3, 80 in 4, 100 in 5. So 20 times 5 is 100, and the wave takes about 5 seconds.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying the speed by the time tells you how far a wave goes, so you can predict when it will reach you.
maths.context: This is about the Mexican wave, where each person stands up just after the person beside them.

maths.problem: Water 4 times as deep carries a long wave about 2 times as fast. Lakshmi's wave took 6 seconds there and back in 1 cm of water. About how long should it take in 4 cm of water?
maths.explain: Twice as fast means it takes half the time. Half of 6 seconds is 3 seconds. This is a prediction, so check it in your own tray.
maths.why_maths: A rule lets you predict a result before you test it, and then the test tells you if the rule works.
maths.context: This is about the Tray Test, where the same push sends a wave across water of different depths.

maths.problem: A tsunami can travel about 800 kilometres in an hour over the deep ocean. Near the shore it slows to about 40 kilometres in an hour. How many times faster is it in the deep ocean?
maths.explain: 40 times 2 is 80. 40 times 20 is 800. So 800 is 20 lots of 40, and the deep-ocean wave is about 20 times faster.
maths.why_maths: Saying 'how many times faster' compares two speeds in one number, which is easier to picture than two big numbers.
maths.context: This is about tsunamis, which slow down as the sea gets shallow.

maths.problem: Your straw wave machine has a straw every 3 cm. There are 50 straws. About how long is the machine?
maths.explain: Each straw takes 3 cm. 50 straws take 50 times 3 cm. 5 times 3 is 15, so 50 times 3 is 150 cm.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying tells you how much tape to cut before you start building.
maths.context: This is about the Straw Wave Machine, made of straws laid across a strip of tape.

roots.context: We have sent waves across water, along a dupatta and through a row of people. Now we ask what waves tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In your tray, the same push sent a wave slowly through shallow water and fast through deeper water. Your hand did the same thing each time. So once a wave starts, the water it travels through sets its speed. That is why a tsunami slows down as the sea gets shallow.
deep_truth.habit: We expect whoever starts something to decide how fast it goes, as a harder throw makes a faster ball. A ball carries its own motion. A wave is passed on by everything it travels through, so they set its pace.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Tray Test, two trips there and back took about 5 seconds in 1 cm of water and about 3 seconds in 4 cm, with the same push. In the family stadium wave, the same start made a slower wave when everyone waited before standing.

three.who_am_i: Your voice reaches a friend as a wave in the air. The air by your mouth stays by your mouth, yet your words arrive.
three.what_is_life: A spider feels waves along her web and runs to her food. A fish feels waves in the water and turns with the shoal. Living beings know their world through the waves that reach them.
three.what_is_this_world: The sea, the ground and the air are full of waves passing through. Nobody has been to the centre of the Earth, yet waves have told us what is there.

roots.thread: Before you tap, the water in the bucket is flat and still. One tap gives it energy, and that energy spreads out as ring after ring of ripples. No ripple is made of new water. Each is the same body of water, rising and falling as the energy passes. So the many ripples are one water, moving in many places.

teachings.teaching: As waves, foam and bubbles are not different from water, so the whole world that comes from the Self is not different from it.
teachings.link: Your tray showed the fact this verse starts from: a wave has no stuff of its own. It is the water itself, moving. The Ashtavakra Gita uses that fact about water to speak about the world.

teachings.teaching: Nothing in the world is softer and weaker than water. Yet nothing is better at wearing down what is hard and strong.
teachings.link: Water gives way to your finger. Yet water passing on the energy of an undersea earthquake broke sea walls in 2004. Water carries energy by giving way, each part passing it to the next.

science.text: Energy is never made or destroyed. A wave carries energy from one place to another. When a wave fades, its energy has turned into a little warmth in the water.
Ripples, sound, earthquake shaking and light look very different, but they are all waves. The same ideas of wavelength and speed describe every one of them.

other_view.view: A wave is only bits of water each pushing on their neighbours. It is a useful idea for describing water, and it does not tell us anything about the world as a whole.

practice.title: The Breath Ripple
practice.say: Fill a steel tumbler with water and put it on the table. Sit close and keep very still. Breathe in slowly. Now breathe out very gently across the top of the water. playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if in a city flat, with the materials listed. Choices made: the Tray Test uses a push from a dosa turner, not lifting the tray, so the push can be kept the same. A tray of 30 cm or more is needed, because in a short tray the wave comes back too fast to time. Timing two trips there and back gives times of a few seconds, long enough to time with a phone. In 1 cm of water the wave fades fast, so the step says to time one trip there and back if it fades, and a torch at a slant makes the wave easy to see as a bright line. The bucket test uses tapping, not stirring, so only waves are made, and the steps say the puffed rice may creep a centimetre or two, which is true. Blowing through a straw is the comparison, because it pushes the water itself. The spring toy is optional, with the dupatta as the home alternative. The straw wave machine needs about 50 straws or card strips, and dough on the straw ends clearly slows the wave. The curd test uses set curd that is eaten afterwards. Nothing in the spine needs a garden, a beach or a living thing.

how_we_found_out.story: In the 1920s, earth scientists studied the waves that big earthquakes send right through the Earth. One kind of earthquake wave cannot pass through liquid, and it never came through the Earth's core. So many scientists thought the whole core was liquid metal. Inge Lehmann, a scientist in Denmark, looked closely at the records of a big earthquake in New Zealand in 1929. Machines far away, on the other side of the Earth, had picked up faint waves in places where a fully liquid core should leave none. She had no computer. She wrote the arrival times on cards and sorted them in boxes, by hand. In 1936 she published a short paper with a title of just two characters, P′. She showed that the faint waves made sense if the liquid core had a solid ball inside it. Waves travel faster in that solid ball, so their paths bend, and some reach places they could not reach otherwise. Other scientists soon agreed with her. In 1970, more sensitive machines picked up waves bouncing off the solid inner core. Inge Lehmann lived to be 104.
how_we_found_out.who: Inge Lehmann (1888 to 1993), a Danish seismologist, a scientist who studies earthquakes
how_we_found_out.when: 1929 (the New Zealand earthquake), 1936 (her paper on the inner core) and 1970 (the confirmation)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many scientists thought the Earth's core was liquid all the way through. Lehmann showed that faint waves arriving where a fully liquid core would leave none were explained by a solid inner core, and later measurements confirmed it.
